q: Some physical quantities of physics are completely described by a single number (or magnitude) with an appropriate unit.
e: This is the exact definition of scalar quantities provided in the text.

q: Quantities that have only magnitude are called vector quantities.
e: Quantities that have only magnitude are called scalar quantities, not vector quantities.

q: Quantities that have both magnitude and direction are called vectors.
e: This is the exact definition of vector quantities provided in the text.

q: The length of a ship being 30 m is an example of a vector quantity.
e: The length of a ship is a scalar quantity because it has only magnitude, no direction.

q: The mass of a block being 500 g is an example of a scalar quantity.
e: Mass is completely described by a single number and unit, making it a scalar.

q: A plane flying with a velocity of 20 mi h⁻¹ towards east is an example of a vector quantity.
e: Velocity requires both magnitude (20 mi h⁻¹) and direction (east) for complete description.

q: A force acting on a body being 20 N upwards is an example of a scalar quantity.
e: Force is a vector quantity because it has both magnitude (20 N) and direction (upwards).

q: In printing, vectors are represented by boldface type, such as $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{v}$, $\mathbf{s}$.
e: This is the standard printing convention for vector symbols as stated in the text.

q: In handwriting, vectors are indicated by placing arrows on the bottom of their symbols.
e: In handwriting, vectors are indicated by placing arrows on the top of their symbols.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude and have the same direction.
e: Equality of vectors requires both equal magnitude and identical direction.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ means $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal in magnitude but have opposite directions.
e: The negative sign indicates the vectors have the same magnitude but opposite directions.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = 2\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is two times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$.
e: The direction of $\vec{A}$ is the same as that of $\vec{B}$, not opposite.

q: The vector relation $\vec{A} = -3\vec{B}$ means the magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is three times the magnitude of $\vec{B}$ and the direction of $\vec{A}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{B}$.
e: The factor of 3 scales the magnitude, and the negative sign reverses the direction.

q: Using graphical method, a vector may be represented by an arrow.
e: An arrow is the standard graphical representation of a vector.

q: The length of the arrow representing a vector is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the vector.
e: The length of the arrow is proportional (directly), not inversely proportional, to the magnitude.

q: To add $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, first draw $\vec{A}$, then draw $\vec{B}$ such that the tail of $\vec{B}$ is at the tip of $\vec{A}$.
e: This describes the correct head-to-tail method for graphical vector addition.

q: The vector sum $\vec{A} + \vec{B}$ is called the resultant vector.
e: The resultant vector is the defined term for the sum of two vectors.

q: The resultant vector is drawn from the tip of $\vec{A}$ to the tail of $\vec{B}$.
e: The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of $\vec{A}$ to the tip of $\vec{B}$.

q: Vector addition is commutative, so $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$.
e: The order of vector addition does not change the resultant vector.

q: In algebraic notation, $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$.
e: Vector subtraction is defined as the addition of the negative of the second vector.

q: To subtract $\vec{B}$ from $\vec{A}$, we add $\vec{A}$ and a vector with the same magnitude as $\vec{B}$ but its direction is the same as that of $\vec{B}$.
e: The direction of the added vector must be opposite to that of $\vec{B}$.

q: Vector subtraction is commutative.
e: Vector subtraction is not commutative; $\vec{A} - \vec{B} \neq \vec{B} - \vec{A}$.

q: The process of sub-dividing a vector into two or more vectors is called resolution of a vector.
e: This is the exact definition of vector resolution provided in the text.

q: The new vectors obtained from resolution are called vector components of the original vector.
e: The subdivided vectors are formally known as vector components.

q: A useful application of vector resolution is sub-dividing a vector into two perpendicular components, namely, horizontal component and vertical component.
e: Resolving into perpendicular x and y components is a primary application.

q: The x-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_x = A \sin \theta$.
e: The x-component (horizontal) is calculated using cosine: $A_x = A \cos \theta$.

q: The y-component of a vector $\vec{A}$ inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the x-axis is $A_y = A \sin \theta$.
e: The y-component (vertical) is correctly calculated using sine.

q: Distance travelled by the body is the length of the path along which the body moves.
e: This is the exact definition of distance provided in the text.

q: Displacement is a scalar directed from the starting point to the end point.
e: Displacement is a vector, not a scalar, because it has both magnitude and direction.

q: Displacement is the distance travelled along a particular direction.
e: This accurately describes displacement as directed distance.

q: Distance has a specific direction.
e: Distance has no specific direction; it has only magnitude.

q: Distance has only magnitude, and therefore, it is a scalar.
e: The lack of directional quality makes distance a scalar quantity.

q: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, and therefore, it is a vector.
e: The presence of both magnitude and specific direction classifies displacement as a vector.

q: The average speed $v_{av}$ is the ratio of total distance $s$ to time taken $t$.
e: This is the correct formula and definition for average speed.

q: The average speed $v_{av}$ is the ratio of total displacement to time taken $t$.
e: Average speed uses total distance, whereas average velocity uses total displacement.

q: The average velocity $v_{av}$ is the ratio of total displacement $s$ to time taken $t$.
e: This is the correct formula and definition for average velocity.

q: If the starting point and the end point are the same, the total displacement is zero.
e: With no net change in position, the displacement vector has zero magnitude.

q: If the starting point and the end point are the same, the average velocity is zero.
e: Since total displacement is zero, the ratio of displacement to time is also zero.

q: The speed and velocity which represent a motion for a certain period of time interval are called average speed and average velocity.
e: This correctly distinguishes average quantities as representing a time interval.

q: The speed or velocity at a particular instant of time are referred to as instantaneous speed and instantaneous velocity.
e: This is the exact definition of instantaneous quantities provided in the text.

q: The speedometer of a car indicates the average speed of the car.
e: The speedometer indicates the instantaneous speed of the car at that particular moment.

q: Instantaneous speed is defined as the time rate of change of distance.
e: This is the limiting value of distance over time as the time interval approaches zero.

q: Instantaneous velocity is defined as the time rate of change of distance.
e: Instantaneous velocity is defined as the time rate of change of displacement, not distance.

q: When a body is moving along a straight line with a constant speed, the velocity of the body is also constant.
e: In straight-line motion, constant speed means both magnitude and direction remain constant.

q: Motion with constant velocity is known as uniform motion.
e: Uniform motion is the defined term for motion with constant velocity.

q: For a motion with constant velocity, equal displacements take place in unequal intervals of time.
e: For constant velocity, equal displacements take place in equal intervals of time.

q: If either magnitude or direction or both magnitude and direction of the velocity changes, the body is said to have an acceleration.
e: Any change in the velocity vector (magnitude, direction, or both) constitutes acceleration.

q: Motion with changing velocity is called non-uniform motion or accelerated motion.
e: These are the correct terms for motion where velocity is not constant.

q: The average acceleration $a_{av}$ is defined by the equation $a_{av} = \frac{v - v_0}{t}$.
e: This is the correct formula for average acceleration, representing change in velocity over time.

q: Average acceleration is the ratio of the change in velocity to the distance taken.
e: Average acceleration is the ratio of the change in velocity to the time taken, not distance.

q: Instantaneous acceleration $a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{dv}{dt}$.
e: This is the correct mathematical definition of instantaneous acceleration.

q: Instantaneous acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity.
e: This is the exact conceptual definition provided in the text.

q: Acceleration is said to be positive if the magnitude of velocity is decreasing.
e: Acceleration is positive if the magnitude of velocity is increasing, not decreasing.

q: Negative acceleration is usually called deceleration or retardation.
e: These are the standard terms used for negative acceleration in the text.

q: Motion along a straight line is called linear motion.
e: This is the exact definition of linear motion provided in the text.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the displacement is equal to the distance moved.
e: Because the path is straight, the path length equals the magnitude of the displacement vector.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the velocity is also equal to the speed.
e: For straight-line motion without direction changes, speed and velocity magnitude are identical.

q: The most simplest type of motion is the linear motion with constant velocity.
e: This is stated explicitly in the text as the simplest type of motion.

q: Since the velocity is constant, the acceleration is non-zero.
e: Since the velocity is constant, there is no change in velocity, so the acceleration is zero.

q: As the body is moving with a non-varying velocity, the instantaneous velocity and average velocity are the same.
e: Constant velocity means the velocity at any instant equals the average over any interval.

q: In describing the equations of motion we shall use the vector notation.
e: The text states we shall not use vector notation, but rather positive and negative signs for direction.

q: We will use positive (+) and negative (-) signs to describe the two opposite directions along a straight line.
e: This is the stated convention for handling direction in 1D equations of motion.

q: The equation of motion for a linear motion with constant velocity is $v = \frac{s}{t}$.
e: This is the fundamental equation for constant velocity motion.

q: If the rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be constant.
e: A constant rate of change of velocity is the definition of constant acceleration.

q: If a body is moving with a constant acceleration of $5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, the velocity of the body changes by $5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in every second.
e: This is the exact example provided in the text to illustrate constant acceleration.

q: Since the acceleration is constant, the instantaneous acceleration and average acceleration are different.
e: Since the acceleration is constant, the instantaneous acceleration and average acceleration are the same.

q: The equation $v = v_0 + at$ is an equation of motion for constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.6), a fundamental equation of motion for constant acceleration.

q: The equation $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$ is an equation of motion for constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.7), relating velocity, acceleration, and displacement without time.

q: The equation $s = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ is derived from other equations of motion.
e: The text explicitly states this equation is derived from Eqs. (2.6), (2.9), and (2.10).

q: The equation $s = \bar{v}t$ is an equation of motion where $\bar{v}$ is average velocity.
e: This is Eq. (2.9), correctly identifying $\bar{v}$ as average velocity.

q: The equation $\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}$ is valid for motion with constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.10), which gives the average velocity for constant acceleration.

q: Except Eq. (2.7), the rest equations can be expressed in vector form.
e: The text explicitly notes that Eq. (2.7) cannot be expressed in vector form, while the others can.

q: The SI unit of displacement is centimetre (cm).
e: The SI (MKS) unit of displacement is the metre (m), while centimetre is the CGS unit.

q: The CGS unit of velocity is $\text{cm s}^{-1}$.
e: This matches the CGS column in Table 2.1 of the text.

q: The FPS unit of acceleration is $\text{ft s}^{-2}$.
e: This matches the FPS column in Table 2.1 of the text.

q: The unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$ means metre per second square.
e: This is the exact verbal description of the SI unit of acceleration provided in the text.

q: Motion can be described or analyzed conveniently with the help of graphs.
e: This is the opening statement of the motion graphs section.

q: The motion graphs are of three types: displacement-time graph, velocity-time graph, and acceleration-time graph.
e: These are the three specific types of motion graphs listed in the text.

q: The motion graphs are of four types.
e: The text explicitly states there are three types of motion graphs, not four.

q: The slope of the s-t graph gives the constant velocity.
e: For linear motion with constant velocity, the slope of the displacement-time graph equals the velocity.

q: Of three types of motion graphs, the s-t graph is very useful to analyze a motion.
e: The text explicitly states that the v-t graph is very useful to analyze a motion.

q: Of three types of motion graphs, the v-t graph is very useful to analyze a motion.
e: This is the exact statement from the text highlighting the utility of the v-t graph.

q: The slope of a v-t graph gives the velocity of a body.
e: The slope of a v-t graph gives the acceleration of a body, not the velocity.

q: The slope of a v-t graph gives the acceleration of a body.
e: This is a key analytical property of the velocity-time graph stated in the text.

q: The area under a v-t graph gives the velocity of a body.
e: The area under a v-t graph gives the displacement or distance moved, not the velocity.

q: The area under a v-t graph gives the displacement or distance moved by the body.
e: This is a key analytical property of the velocity-time graph stated in the text.

q: A negative slope on a v-t graph indicates positive acceleration.
e: A negative slope indicates negative acceleration, also known as retardation.

q: A negative slope on a v-t graph indicates negative acceleration or retardation.
e: This correctly interprets the physical meaning of a negative slope on a velocity-time graph.
